content.narrative_summary: This section describes the purpose and scope of the ESC Guidelines: they evaluate and summarize evidence to assist health professionals in selecting the best diagnostic and therapeutic approaches for individual patients. The Guidelines are intended for use by health professionals, freely available through the European Society of Cardiology (ESC), and do not override individual professional responsibility to make appropriate, accurate decisions in consultation with patients or caregivers. The Guidelines represent the official ESC position on a topic, are regularly updated when new evidence emerges (this version replaces the 2020 guideline), and the task force selection process aimed for diversity across ESC regions.

content.title: 2.1. What is new
content.narrative_summary: This section presents new recommendations across multiple domains including diagnostic evaluation, AF-CARE principles, comorbidity and risk factor management, initiation and maintenance of oral anticoagulation, and antiplatelet strategies.

recommendation_tables.title: Table 3 New recommendations

rows.recommendation: A transthoracic echocardiogram is recommended in patients with an AF diagnosis where this will guide treatment decisions.

Education directed to patients, family members, caregivers, and healthcare professionals is recommended to optimize shared decision-making, facilitating open discussion of both the benefit and risk associated with each treatment option.

Access to patient-centred management according to the AF-CARE principles is recommended in all patients with AF, regardless of gender, ethnicity, and socioeconomic status, to ensure equality in healthcare provision and improve outcomes.
Patient-centred AF management with a multidisciplinary approach should be considered in all patients with AF to optimize management and improve outcomes.
Diuretics are recommended in patients with AF, HF, and congestion to alleviate symptoms and facilitate better AF management.
Appropriate medical therapy for HF is recommended in AF patients with HF and impaired LVEF to reduce symptoms and/or HF hospitalization and prevent AF recurrence.

Sodium-glucose cotransporter-2 inhibitors are recommended for patients with HF and AF regardless of left ventricular ejection fraction to reduce the risk of HF hospitalization and cardiovascular death.
Effective glycaemic control is recommended as part of comprehensive risk factor management in individuals with diabetes mellitus and AF, to reduce burden, recurrence, and progression of AF.

Bariatric surgery may be considered in conjunction with lifestyle changes and weight management in individuals with AF and body mass index ≥40 kg/m2 c where a rhythm control strategy is planned, to reduce recurrence and progression of AF.
Management of obstructive sleep apnoea may be considered as part of a comprehensive management of risk factors in individuals with AF to reduce recurrence and progression.
When screening for obstructive sleep apnoea in individuals with AF, using only symptom-based questionnaires is not recommended.
Oral anticoagulation is recommended in patients with clinical AF at elevated thromboembolic risk to prevent ischaemic stroke and thromboembolism.
A CHA₂DS₂-VA score of 2 or more is recommended as an indicator of elevated thromboembolic risk for decisions on initiating oral anticoagulation.
A CHA₂DS₂-VA score of 1 should be considered an indicator of elevated thromboembolic risk for decisions on initiating oral anticoagulation.
Oral anticoagulation is recommended in all patients with AF and hypertrophic cardiomyopathy or cardiac amyloidosis, regardless of CHA₂DS₂-VA score, to prevent ischaemic stroke and thromboembolism.
Individualized reassessment of thromboembolic risk is recommended at periodic intervals in patients with AF to ensure anticoagulation is started in appropriate patients.

Direct oral anticoagulant therapy may be considered in patients with asymptomatic device-detected subclinical AF and elevated thromboembolic risk to prevent ischaemic stroke and thromboembolism, excluding patients at high risk of bleeding.
A reduced dose of DOAC therapy is not recommended, unless patients meet DOAC-specific criteria, to prevent underdosing and avoidable thromboembolic events.
Maintaining VKA treatment rather than switching to a DOAC may be considered in patients aged ≥75 years on clinically stable therapeutic VKA with polypharmacy to prevent excess bleeding risk.
Adding antiplatelet treatment to oral anticoagulation is not recommended in AF patients for the goal of preventing ischaemic stroke or thromboembolism.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations

rows.recommendation: A thorough diagnostic work-up should be considered in patients taking an oral anticoagulant and presenting with ischaemic stroke or thromboembolism to prevent recurrent events, including assessment of non-cardioembolic causes, vascular risk factors, dosage, and adherence.
Adding antiplatelet treatment to anticoagulation is not recommended in patients with AF to prevent recurrent embolic stroke.
Switching from one DOAC to another, or from a DOAC to a VKA, without a clear indication is not recommended in patients with AF to prevent recurrent embolic stroke.

Surgical closure of the left atrial appendage should be considered as an adjunct to oral anticoagulation in patients with AF undergoing endoscopic or hybrid AF ablation to prevent ischaemic stroke and thromboembolism.

Stand-alone endoscopic surgical closure of the left atrial appendage may be considered in patients with AF and contraindications for long-term anticoagulant treatment to prevent ischaemic stroke and thromboembolism.
Specific antidotes should be considered in AF patients on a DOAC who develop a life-threatening bleed, or bleed into a critical site, to reverse the antithrombotic effect.

Rate control therapy is recommended in patients with AF, as initial therapy in the acute setting, an adjunct to rhythm control therapies, or as a sole treatment strategy to control heart rate and reduce symptoms.
Beta-blockers, diltiazem, verapamil, or digoxin are recommended as first-choice drugs in patients with AF and LVEF >40% to control heart rate and reduce symptoms.

Atrioventricular node ablation combined with cardiac resynchronization therapy should be considered in severely symptomatic patients with permanent AF and at least one hospitalization for HF to reduce symptoms, physical limitations, recurrent HF hospitalization, and mortality.
Direct oral anticoagulants are recommended in preference to VKAs in eligible patients with AF undergoing cardioversion for thromboembolic risk reduction.
Cardioversion of AF (either electrical or pharmacological) should be considered in symptomatic patients with persistent AF as part of a rhythm control approach.

A wait-and-see approach for spontaneous conversion to sinus rhythm within 48 h of AF onset should be considered in patients without haemodynamic compromise as an alternative to immediate cardioversion.

Implementation of a rhythm control strategy should be considered within 12 months of diagnosis in selected patients with AF at risk of thromboembolic events to reduce the risk of cardiovascular death or hospitalization.

Early cardioversion is not recommended without appropriate anticoagulation or transoesophageal echocardiography if AF duration is longer than 24 h, or there is scope to wait for spontaneous cardioversion.

Electrical cardioversion as a diagnostic tool should be considered in patients with persistent AF where there is uncertainty about the value of sinus rhythm restoration on symptoms, or to assess improvement in left ventricular function.
Antiarrhythmic drug therapy is not recommended in patients with advanced conduction disturbances unless antibradycardia pacing is provided.
Atrial fibrillation catheter ablation should be considered in patients with AF-related bradycardia or sinus pauses on AF termination to improve symptoms and avoid pacemaker implantation.

Repeat AF catheter ablation should be considered in patients with AF recurrence after initial catheter ablation, provided the patient’s symptoms were improved after the initial PVI or after failed initial PVI, to reduce symptoms, recurrence, and progression of AF.
Uninterrupted oral anticoagulation is recommended in patients undergoing AF catheter ablation to prevent peri-procedural ischaemic stroke and thromboembolism.

rows.recommendation: Review of an ECG (12-lead, single, or multiple leads) by a physician is recommended to provide a definite diagnosis of AF and commence appropriate management.

Population-based screening for AF using a prolonged non-invasive ECG-based approach should be considered in individuals aged ≥75 years, or ≥65 years with additional CHA₂DS₂-VA risk factors to ensure earlier detection of AF.

recommendation_tables.title: Primary prevention of AF—Section 10.5

rows.recommendation: Maintaining optimal blood pressure is recommended in the general population to prevent AF, with ACE inhibitors or ARBs as first-line therapy.
Appropriate medical HF therapy is recommended in individuals with HFrEF to prevent AF.
Maintaining normal weight (BMI 20–25 kg/m2) is recommended for the general population to prevent AF.
Maintaining an active lifestyle is recommended to prevent AF, with the equivalent of 150–300 min per week of moderate intensity or 75–150 min per week of vigorous intensity aerobic physical activity.
Avoidance of binge drinking and alcohol excess is recommended in the general population to prevent AF.
Metformin or SGLT2 inhibitors should be considered for individuals needing pharmacological management of diabetes mellitus to prevent AF.
Weight reduction should be considered in obese individuals to prevent AF.

recommendation_tables.title: Table 4 Revised recommendations

rows.recommendation: Confirmation by an electrocardiogram (12-lead, multiple, or single leads) is recommended to establish the diagnosis of clinical AF and commence risk stratification and treatment.
rows.supporting_text: ECG documentation is required to establish the diagnosis of AF. A standard 12-lead ECG recording or a single-lead ECG tracing of ≥30 s showing heart rhythm with no discernible repeating P waves and irregular RR intervals (when atrioventricular conduction is not impaired) is diagnostic of clinical AF.

rows.recommendation: Evaluating the impact of AF-related symptoms is recommended before and after major changes in treatment to inform shared decision-making and guide treatment choices.
rows.supporting_text:
In patients with AF, it is recommended to:
 • Evaluate AF-related symptoms (including fatigue, tiredness, exertional shortness of breath, palpitations, and chest pain) and quantify the patient symptom status using the modified EHRA symptom scale before and after initiation of treatment.
 • Evaluate AF-related symptoms before and after cardioversion of persistent AF to aid rhythm control treatment decisions.

rows.recommendation: Blood pressure lowering treatment is recommended in patients with AF and hypertension to reduce recurrence and progression of AF and prevent adverse cardiovascular events.
rows.supporting_text: Attention to good BP control is recommended in AF patients with hypertension to reduce AF recurrences and risk of stroke and bleeding.

rows.recommendation: Weight loss is recommended as part of comprehensive risk factor management in overweight and obese individuals with AF to reduce symptoms and AF burden, with a target of 10% or more reduction in body weight.
rows.supporting_text: In obese patients with AF, weight loss together with management of other risk factors should be considered to reduce AF incidence, AF progression, AF recurrences, and symptoms.

rows.recommendation: A tailored exercise programme is recommended in individuals with paroxysmal or persistent AF to improve cardiorespiratory fitness and reduce AF recurrence.
rows.supporting_text: Physical activity should be considered to help prevent AF incidence or recurrence, with the exception of excessive endurance exercise, which may promote AF.

rows.recommendation: Reducing alcohol consumption to ≤3 standard drinks (≤30 grams of alcohol) per week is recommended as part of comprehensive risk factor management to reduce AF recurrence.
rows.supporting_text: Advice and management to avoid alcohol excess should be considered for AF prevention and in AF patients considered for OAC therapy.

rows.recommendation: Surgical closure of the left atrial appendage is recommended as an adjunct to oral anticoagulation in patients with AF undergoing cardiac surgery to prevent ischaemic stroke and thromboembolism.
rows.supporting_text: Surgical occlusion or exclusion of the LAA may be considered for stroke prevention in patients with AF undergoing cardiac surgery.

rows.recommendation: Assessment and management of modifiable bleeding risk factors is recommended in all patients eligible for oral anticoagulation, as part of shared decision-making to ensure safety and prevent bleeding.
rows.supporting_text: For a formal risk-score-based assessment of bleeding risk, the HAS-BLED score should be considered to help address modifiable bleeding risk factors, and to identify patients at high risk of bleeding (HAS-BLED score ≥3) for early and more frequent clinical review and follow-up.

section_headings: Section 7.2—Rhythm control strategies in patients with AF
content.narrative_summary: The section defines atrial fibrillation (AF) as a supraventricular arrhythmia with uncoordinated atrial activation leading to loss of effective atrial contraction, absent P waves, and irregular ventricular activation without atrioventricular block. It notes that AF classification is based on temporal patterns (see Table 5) but cautions these categories reflect observed episodes rather than underlying pathophysiology, and patients may progress or require reclassification. The text discusses atrial and ventricular damage in AF, the rationale for retaining the 'permanent' AF definition, the limited evidence for driver‐based classifications, emerging pathology‐based strategies for personalized management, and consensus updates to definitions (see Table 6).

recommendation_tables.title: Section 7.2—Rhythm control strategies in patients with AF

rows.recommendation: AF catheter ablation for PVI should/may be considered as first-line rhythm control therapy to improve symptoms in selected patients with symptomatic: • Paroxysmal AF episodes.
Catheter ablation is recommended as a first-line option within a shared decision-making rhythm control strategy in patients with paroxysmal AF, to reduce symptoms, recurrence, and progression of AF.

Thoracoscopic procedures—including hybrid surgical ablation—should be considered in patients who have symptomatic paroxysmal or persistent AF refractory to AAD therapy and have failed percutaneous AF ablation, or with evident risk factors for catheter ablation failure, to maintain long-term sinus rhythm. The decision must be supported by an experienced team of electrophysiologists and surgeons.

Endoscopic and hybrid ablation procedures may be considered in patients with symptomatic paroxysmal AF refractory to AAD therapy and failed percutaneous catheter ablation strategy to prevent symptoms, recurrence, and progression of AF, within a shared decision-making rhythm control team of electrophysiologists and surgeons.

Thoracoscopic procedures—including hybrid surgical ablation—may be considered in patients with persistent AF with risk factors for recurrence, who remain symptomatic during AF despite at least one failed AAD and who prefer further rhythm control therapy.

Endoscopic and hybrid ablation procedures should be considered in patients with symptomatic persistent AF refractory to AAD therapy to prevent symptoms, recurrence, and progression of AF, within a shared decision-making rhythm control team of electrophysiologists and surgeons.

Concomitant AF ablation should be considered in patients undergoing cardiac surgery, balancing the benefits of freedom from atrial arrhythmias and the risk factors for recurrence (left atrial dilatation, years in AF, age, renal dysfunction, and other cardiovascular risk factors).

Concomitant surgical ablation is recommended in patients undergoing mitral valve surgery and AF suitable for a rhythm control strategy to prevent symptoms and recurrence of AF, with shared decision-making supported by an experienced team of electrophysiologists and arrhythmia surgeons.

recommendation_tables.title: Section 9.6—Post‐operative AF

rows.recommendation: Long-term OAC therapy to prevent thromboembolic events may be considered in patients at risk for stroke with post-operative AF after cardiac surgery, considering the anticipated net clinical benefit of OAC therapy and informed patient preferences.

Long-term oral anticoagulation should be considered in patients with post-operative AF after cardiac and non-cardiac surgery at elevated thromboembolic risk, to prevent ischaemic stroke and thromboembolism.

content.narrative_summary: Atrial fibrillation is associated with serious adverse events, including a high rate of hospitalization and complications. The most common non-fatal outcome is heart failure (RR 4.62; 95% CI, 3.13–6.83), followed by ischaemic stroke, ischaemic heart disease (RR 1.61; 95% CI, 1.38–1.87), and other arterial thromboembolic events; venous thromboembolism is also implicated.

content.title: 5. [C] Comorbidity and risk factor management
content.narrative_summary: A broad array of comorbidities are associated with the recurrence and progression of AF. Managing comorbidities including hypertension, heart failure, diabetes mellitus, obesity, and sleep apnoea—as well as lifestyle changes to improve physical activity and reduce alcohol intake—is central to AF care. Identification and treatment of these comorbidities and risk clusters are important to effective AF-CARE.

content.title: Recommendation Table 5 — Recommendations for comorbidity and risk factor management in AF (see also Evidence Table 5)
content.narrative_summary: The page presents narrative on hypertension and heart failure in patients with atrial fibrillation (AF). The hypertension section describes increased risk of stroke, heart failure, major bleeding, and cardiovascular mortality in AF, recommends a systolic blood pressure target of 120–129 mmHg (with more lenient targets for frail or elderly patients), and an on-treatment diastolic BP of 70–79 mmHg. It notes that a 5 mmHg systolic reduction reduces major cardiovascular events by 9%, and suggests ACE inhibitors or ARBs may be superior for AF recurrence prevention. The heart failure section highlights HF as a key prognostic determinant in AF, with high rates of concomitant AF in new HF cases, increased stroke and mortality risks, and worse outcomes with reduced LVEF. It emphasizes following ESC guidelines (2023 Focused Update) for diagnosis and treatment, achieving euvolaemia with diuretics to aid rate control, and notes limited evidence for many HF therapies in coexisting AF, with conflicting data on ACE inhibitors/ARBs. The narrative ends mid-sentence, indicating continuation on the next page.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendation Table 5 — Recommendations for comorbidity and risk factor management in AF (see also Evidence Table 5)

rows.recommendation: Identification and management of risk factors and comorbidities is recommended as an integral part of AF care.
Blood pressure lowering treatment is recommended in patients with AF and hypertension to reduce recurrence and progression of AF and prevent adverse cardiovascular events.
Diuretics are recommended in patients with AF, HF, and congestion to alleviate symptoms and facilitate better AF management.
Appropriate medical therapy for HF is recommended in AF patients with HF and impaired LVEF to reduce symptoms and/or HF hospitalization and prevent AF recurrence.

Sodium-glucose cotransporter-2 inhibitors are recommended for patients with HF and AF regardless of left ventricular ejection fraction to reduce the risk of HF hospitalization and cardiovascular death.
Effective glycaemic control is recommended as part of comprehensive risk factor management in individuals with diabetes mellitus and AF, to reduce burden, recurrence, and progression of AF.

Weight loss is recommended as part of comprehensive risk factor management in overweight and obese individuals with AF to reduce symptoms and AF burden, with a target of 10% or more reduction in body weight.
A tailored exercise programme is recommended in individuals with paroxysmal or persistent AF to improve cardiorespiratory fitness and reduce AF recurrence.
Reducing alcohol consumption to ≤3 standard drinks (≤30 grams of alcohol) per week is recommended as part of comprehensive risk factor management to reduce AF recurrence.

Bariatric surgery may be considered in conjunction with lifestyle changes and medical management in individuals with AF and body mass index ≥40 kg/m² c where a rhythm control strategy is planned, to reduce recurrence and progression of AF.
Management of obstructive sleep apnoea may be considered as part of a comprehensive management of risk factors in individuals with AF to reduce recurrence and progression.
When screening for obstructive sleep apnoea in individuals with AF, using only symptom-based questionnaires is not recommended.

Section 5.6 highlights the relationship between reduced cardiorespiratory fitness and AF recurrence post-ablation, noting that improved fitness is associated with lower AF burden.

content.title: 6.2. Oral anticoagulants
content.narrative_summary: Vitamin K antagonists such as warfarin have been the principal drugs to prevent thromboembolic events in AF but carry risks of intracranial and major bleeding and require monitoring. The shift to DOACs as first-line therapy reduces the need for routine monitoring. Awareness of potential interactions between VKAs or DOACs and other drugs, foods, and supplements is essential.

figures_tables_algorithms.label: Figure 9
figures_tables_algorithms.title: Common drug interactions with oral anticoagulants
figures_tables_algorithms.summary: A matrix of common or major drug interactions organized by oral anticoagulant class: Vitamin K antagonists and direct oral anticoagulants (apixaban, dabigatran, edoxaban, rivaroxaban). Interaction categories include: avoid where possible, reduce dose, increase dose, monitor INR (for VKAs), delay or reduce DOAC dose, and limit consumption (e.g., grapefruit juice, St John’s wort).

content.narrative_summary: The DOACs (apixaban, dabigatran, edoxaban, rivaroxaban) are non-inferior to warfarin for prevention of thromboembolism in AF and reduce intracranial hemorrhage by about 50%. Meta-analyses of RCTs and post-marketing data confirm lower rates of stroke, systemic embolism, mortality, and ICH with DOACs compared to warfarin, with similar major bleeding. DOACs show benefit in cardioversion, heart failure, older patients, and mild-to-moderate CKD, with dosing adjustments for renal impairment. They are contraindicated in mechanical heart valves and moderate-to-severe mitral stenosis, and specific dose reduction criteria should be used. Routine laboratory testing of DOAC levels is not recommended, though may be helpful in certain clinical situations; patient involvement in decision-making is emphasized.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendation Table 7 — Recommendations for oral anticoagulation in AF (see also Evidence Table 7)

rows.recommendation: Direct oral anticoagulants are recommended in preference to VKAs to prevent ischaemic stroke and thromboembolism, except in patients with mechanical heart valves or moderate-to-severe mitral stenosis.
A target INR of 2.0–3.0 is recommended for patients with AF prescribed a VKA for stroke prevention to ensure safety and effectiveness.

Switching to a DOAC is recommended for eligible patients that have failed to maintain an adequate time in therapeutic range on a VKA (TTR <70%) to prevent thromboembolism and intracranial haemorrhage.

Keeping the time in therapeutic range above 70% should be considered in patients taking a VKA to ensure safety and effectiveness, with INR checks at appropriate frequency and patient-directed education and counselling.
Maintaining VKA treatment rather than switching to a DOAC may be considered in patients aged ≥75 years on clinically stable therapeutic VKA with polypharmacy to prevent excess bleeding risk.
A reduced dose of DOAC therapy is not recommended, unless patients meet DOAC-specific criteria, to prevent underdosing and avoidable thromboembolic events.

content.narrative_summary: Section 6.2.2 discusses Vitamin K antagonists (VKAs), noting that warfarin reduces stroke risk by 64% and mortality by 26% in patients with AF at elevated thromboembolic risk. VKAs remain the only option for AF patients with mechanical heart valves or moderate-to-severe mitral stenosis, require frequent INR monitoring to maintain TTR >70% (INR 2.0–3.0), and are associated with higher rates of intracranial and other bleeding compared with DOACs. Switching from VKAs to DOACs is justified when TTR is <70%, in cases of intracranial bleeding concerns, patient preference, polypharmacy, or older age, though a recent trial in older patients showed increased bleeding when switching. Section 6.2.3 covers clinical versus device-detected subclinical AF, summarizing the ARTESiA trial (apixaban vs aspirin in 4,012 patients with device-detected subclinical AF; mean follow-up 3.5 years; stroke/systemic embolism HR 0.63 [95% CI 0.45–0.88]; P = .007; major bleeding HR 1.36 [95% CI 1.01–1.82]; P = .04) and the NOAH trial (edoxaban stopped early; analysis of 2,536 patients over median 21 months; efficacy HR 0.81 [95% CI 0.60–1.08]; P = .15; death or major bleeding HR 1.31 [95% CI 1.02–1.67]; P = .03), noting low burden of device-detected subclinical AF in both studies.

section_headings: 6.3. Antiplatelet drugs and combinations with anticoagulants
6.4. Residual ischaemic stroke risk despite anticoagulation
content.narrative_summary: Section 6.3 discusses that antiplatelet agents such as aspirin and clopidogrel should not replace oral anticoagulation for stroke prevention in atrial fibrillation and that combined antiplatelet and anticoagulant therapy increases bleeding risk with no clear stroke prevention benefit except in selected acute vascular disease contexts. Section 6.4 highlights that despite effective oral anticoagulation a residual risk of ischaemic stroke persists due to non-AF mechanisms, subtherapeutic dosing, nonadherence or concurrent vascular pathology; routine switching between anticoagulant types or adding antiplatelet therapy is not supported by consistent evidence.

Adding antiplatelet treatment to anticoagulation is not recommended in patients with AF to prevent recurrent embolic stroke.
Switching from one DOAC to another, or from a DOAC to a VKA, without a clear indication is not recommended in patients with AF to prevent recurrent embolic stroke.

section_headings: 6.7.2. Management of bleeding on anticoagulant therapy
content.narrative_summary: The section outlines the importance of identifying and managing modifiable bleeding risk factors when initiating antithrombotic therapy, noting that specific bleeding-risk scores are not universally recommended due to modest predictive ability. General management of active anticoagulant‐related bleeding includes site confirmation, severity assessment, appropriate laboratory testing (e.g., INR for VKAs, specific DOAC assays), and tailored interventions: temporary OAC withdrawal for minor bleeding, fresh frozen plasma or prothrombin concentrates for VKA‐related bleeding, and agents such as charcoal or idarucizumab for DOACs.

Stand-alone endoscopic surgical closure of the left atrial appendage may be considered in patients with AF and contraindications for long-term anticoagulant treatment to prevent ischaemic stroke and thromboembolism.

content.narrative_summary: This figure presents an algorithmic approach (Figure 10) for modifying bleeding risk associated with oral anticoagulant (OAC) therapy. content.narrative_summary: Left column narrative discusses management of bleeding in anticoagulated patients: use of andexanet alfa to reverse factor Xa inhibitors, limited availability of DOAC-specific antidotes, need for institutional multidisciplinary policies, patient education on bleeding signs, and decisions on reinstating oral anticoagulation balanced against bleeding severity and thromboembolic risk. recommendation_tables.title: Recommendation Table 13 — Recommendations for management of bleeding in anticoagulated patients (see also Evidence Table 13)

rows.recommendation: Interrupting anticoagulation and performing diagnostic or treatment interventions is recommended in AF patients with active bleeding until the cause of bleeding is identified and resolved.
Prothrombin complex concentrates should be considered in AF patients on VKAs who develop a life-threatening bleed, or bleed into a critical site, to reverse the antithrombotic effect.
Specific antidotes should be considered in AF patients on a DOAC who develop a life-threatening bleed, or bleed into a critical site, to reverse the antithrombotic effect.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendation Table 14 — Recommendations for heart rate control in patients with AF (see also Evidence Table 14)

rows.recommendation: Rate control therapy is recommended in patients with AF, as initial therapy in the acute setting, and adjunct to rhythm control therapies, or as a sole treatment strategy to control heart rate and reduce symptoms.
Beta-blockers, diltiazem, verapamil, or digoxin are recommended as first-choice drugs in patients with AF and LVEF >40% to control heart rate and reduce symptoms.
Beta-blockers and/or digoxin are recommended in patients with AF and LVEF <40% to control heart rate and reduce symptoms.

Combination rate control therapy should be considered if a single drug does not control symptoms or heart rate in patients with AF, providing that bradycardia can be avoided, to control heart rate and reduce symptoms.

Lenient rate control with a resting heart rate of <110 b.p.m. should be considered as the initial target for patients with AF, with stricter control reserved for those with continuing AF-related symptoms.

Atrioventricular node ablation in combination with pacemaker implantation should be considered in patients unresponsive to, or ineligible for, intensive rate and rhythm control therapy to control heart rate and reduce symptoms.

Atrioventricular node ablation combined with cardiac resynchronization therapy should be considered in severely symptomatic patients with permanent AF and at least one hospitalization for HF to reduce symptoms, physical limitations, recurrent HF hospitalizations, and mortality.
Intravenous amiodarone, digoxin, or landiolol may be considered in patients with AF who have haemodynamic instability or severely depressed LVEF to achieve acute control of heart rate.

section_headings: 7.1.2 Heart rate control in the acute setting
content.narrative_summary: Section 7.1.1 describes that optimal rate control in AF depends on setting, symptom burden, heart failure presence, and whether combined with rhythm control. The RACE II trial supports a lenient target (<110 b.p.m.) as non-inferior to strict control (<80 b.p.m. at rest; <110 b.p.m. during exercise) for clinical outcomes. Section 7.1.2 emphasizes evaluating and managing underlying causes before or alongside acute rate control, with beta-blockers and diltiazem/verapamil preferred for most, and digoxin reserved for specific situations (e.g., cardiogenic shock); combination therapy requires close monitoring. Section 7.1.3 notes that long-term pharmacological rate control can be achieved with beta-blockers, diltiazem, verapamil, digoxin, or combination therapy.

content.narrative_summary: This page summarizes evidence from major trials (dronedarone studies, CASTLE-AF, CASTLE-HTx, CABANA, EAST-AFNET 4) demonstrating that a rhythm control strategy in atrial fibrillation (AF) can reduce cardiovascular morbidity and mortality. The task force concludes that rhythm control should be instituted to alleviate AF-related symptoms and potentially improve outcomes, while acknowledging the inherent thromboembolic risk. Recommendations on cardioversion emphasize at least 3 weeks of therapeutic oral anticoagulation (or transoesophageal echocardiography if shorter), continuation of anticoagulation for ≥4 weeks post-procedure, and criteria for early versus delayed cardioversion.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendation Table 15 — Recommendations for general concepts in rhythm control (see also Evidence Table 15)

rows.recommendation: Electrical cardioversion is recommended in AF patients with acute or worsening haemodynamic instability to improve immediate patient outcomes.
Direct oral anticoagulants are recommended in preference to VKAs in eligible patients with AF undergoing cardioversion for thromboembolic risk reduction.

content.narrative_summary: Electrical cardioversion (ECV) can be safely applied electively and acutely with sedation using agents such as midazolam, propofol, or etomidate. Integrated care for recent-onset AF at the emergency department improves outcomes without compromising safety, and major adverse events are lower with DOACs versus warfarin. Blood pressure monitoring and oximetry should be routine; atropine, isoproterenol, or temporary pacing should be available for bradycardia. Biphasic defibrillators are preferred, and no single optimal electrode position exists. Active pad compression and fixed-energy shocks improve success rates over escalating-energy protocols. Pretreatment with vernakalant, flecainide, ibutilide, propafenone, or amiodarone for 3–4 days enhances ECV success and long-term sinus rhythm maintenance; meta-analyses support amiodarone pre- and post-treatment. In persistent AF, ECV may help assess arrhythmia impact on symptoms and LV function in patients with HFrEF. Pharmacological cardioversion is less effective than ECV; success is influenced by timing and may be biased by spontaneous conversion.

content.narrative_summary: The long-term effectiveness of antiarrhythmic drugs (AADs) for AF is limited; meta-analyses show 20–50% reduction in recurrences but no mortality benefit except potential signals with sotalol and amiodarone. Shared decision-making and careful evaluation of safety profiles (proarrhythmia, organ toxicity) should guide AAD selection and dosing. Catheter ablation reduces AF recurrences, burden, and improves quality of life in symptomatic paroxysmal or persistent AF when AADs are intolerable or ineffective. Multiple RCTs support first-line ablation in paroxysmal AF with similar adverse event rates to AADs; its superiority in persistent AF is unclear. Pulmonary vein isolation remains the cornerstone; emerging techniques (e.g., pulsed field ablation) show promise. Delaying ablation by up to 12 months may not affect arrhythmia-free survival. Only select asymptomatic patients may be candidates. In HFrEF patients, ablation reduces arrhythmia recurrence, improves ejection fraction, and may enhance clinical outcomes.

section_headings: 9.4. AF-CARE in acute stroke or intracranial haemorrhage
content.narrative_summary:
The evidence for ACS treated without revascularization is limited; six to 12 months of a single antiplatelet agent plus a long-term DOAC is usually sufficient and may minimize bleeding risk. In stable CCS patients beyond 12 months, DOAC monotherapy is adequate without additional antiplatelet therapy. Proton pump inhibitors are reasonable during combined antithrombotic therapy for patients at gastrointestinal bleeding risk, and multimorbid ACS or CCS patients require comprehensive ischaemic and bleeding risk assessment to tailor therapy.

Section 9.3: Peripheral arterial disease (PAD) affects 6.7–14% of AF patients and predicts higher stroke and mortality. DOACs are preferred for long-term anticoagulation in chronic PAD. After endovascular revascularization, combination with single antiplatelet therapy should be as brief as possible (approximately 1 month for peripheral procedures and 90 days for neuro-interventional procedures).

Section 9.4.1: Management of acute ischaemic stroke in AF patients on OAC is beyond the scope of these guidelines; therapy depends on regimen and intensity of OAC and should be coordinated by a specialist neurologist team according to relevant guidelines.

content.narrative_summary: The timing of starting or restarting oral anticoagulation (OAC) after ischaemic stroke remains unclear. Low-dose aspirin within 48 h is recommended, and randomized trials (ELAN, TIMING) found early direct OAC use non-inferior to delayed initiation, with ongoing trials planned. There is insufficient evidence to guide OAC initiation after intracerebral haemorrhage; small trials (APACHE-AF, SoSTART) showed no difference in long-term stroke or mortality, and further data are awaited. Trigger-induced AF is defined as new AF associated with reversible factors, and the task force adopts the term AF-CARE for its management pathway.

content.narrative_summary: The page continues discussion of AF screening trials, including prolonged single-lead ECG monitoring and the LOOP implantable recorder trial, showing modest detection benefits but no significant reduction in stroke or mortality. Meta-analyses of RCTs suggest a small benefit of prolonged screening, though results are underpowered for key clinical outcomes. Section 10.4 introduces risk predictors for incident AF, noting observational associations and Mendelian randomization evidence implicating systolic blood pressure and BMI. Section 10.5 begins with the rationale for primary prevention of AF by targeting modifiable risk factors, with evidence for interventions in hypertension, heart failure, type 2 diabetes, obesity, and sleep apnoea syndrome.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendation Table 32 — Recommendations for primary prevention of AF (see also Evidence Table 32)

rows.recommendation: Maintaining optimal blood pressure is recommended in the general population to prevent AF, with ACE inhibitors or ARBs as first-line therapy.
Appropriate medical HF therapy is recommended in individuals with HFrEF to prevent AF.
Maintaining normal weight (BMI 20–25 kg/m2) is recommended for the general population to prevent AF.
Maintaining an active lifestyle is recommended to prevent AF, with the equivalent of 150–300 min per week of moderate intensity or 75–150 min per week of vigorous intensity aerobic physical activity.
Avoidance of binge drinking and alcohol excess is recommended in the general population to prevent AF.
Metformin or SGLT2 inhibitors should be considered for individuals needing pharmacological management of diabetes mellitus to prevent AF.
Weight reduction should be considered in obese individuals to prevent AF.

content.narrative_summary: The page reports that observational and cohort studies link reduced alcohol consumption to lower incidence of atrial fibrillation. It then presents 25 key messages outlining optimal AF management across the AF-CARE pathway (including diagnosis, comorbidity management, anticoagulation, rate and rhythm control, ablation, and dynamic reassessment) and identifies major gaps in evidence: variability in AF progression/regression, need for validated clinical definitions, treatment strategy uncertainties, incomplete understanding of diverse pathophysiology and comorbidities, and challenges in personalized risk prediction.

content.title: 13. ‘What to do’ and ‘What not to do’ messages from the guidelines
section_headings: 13. ‘What to do’ and ‘What not to do’ messages from the guidelines
content.narrative_summary: Table 17 presents Class I and Class III recommendations (‘what to do’ and ‘what not to do’) for atrial fibrillation management alongside their levels of evidence.

recommendation_tables.title: ‘What to do’ and ‘what not to do’

rows.recommendation: Confirmation by an electrocardiogram (12-lead, multiple, or single leads) is recommended to establish the diagnosis of clinical AF and commence risk stratification and treatment.
Evaluating the impact of AF-related symptoms is recommended before and after major changes in treatment to inform shared decision-making and guide treatment choices.
A transthoracic echocardiogram is recommended in patients with an AF diagnosis where this will guide treatment decisions.

Education directed to patients, family members, caregivers, and healthcare professionals is recommended to optimize shared decision-making, facilitating open discussion of both the benefit and risk associated with each treatment option.

Access to patient-centred management according to the AF-CARE principles is recommended in all patients with AF, regardless of gender, ethnicity, and socioeconomic status, to ensure equality in healthcare provision and improve outcomes.
Identification and management of risk factors and comorbidities is recommended as an integral part of AF care.
Blood pressure lowering treatment is recommended in patients with AF and hypertension to reduce recurrence and progression of AF and prevent adverse cardiovascular events.
Diuretics are recommended in patients with AF, HF, and congestion to alleviate symptoms and facilitate better AF management.
Appropriate medical therapy for HF is recommended in AF patients with HF and impaired LVEF to reduce symptoms and/or HF hospitalization and prevent AF recurrence.

Sodium-glucose cotransporter-2 inhibitors are recommended for patients with HF and AF regardless of left ventricular ejection fraction to reduce the risk of HF hospitalization and cardiovascular death.
Effective glycaemic control is recommended as part of comprehensive risk factor management in individuals with diabetes mellitus and AF, to reduce burden, recurrence, and progression of AF.

Weight loss is recommended as part of comprehensive risk factor management in overweight and obese individuals with AF to reduce symptoms and AF burden, with a target of 10% or more reduction in body weight.
A tailored exercise programme is recommended in individuals with paroxysmal or persistent AF to improve cardiorespiratory fitness and reduce AF recurrence.
Reducing alcohol consumption to ≤3 standard drinks (≤30 grams of alcohol) per week is recommended as part of comprehensive risk factor management to reduce AF recurrence.
When screening for obstructive sleep apnoea in individuals with AF, using only symptom-based questionnaires is not recommended.
Oral anticoagulation is recommended in patients with clinical AF at elevated thromboembolic risk to prevent ischaemic stroke and thromboembolism.
A CHA2DS2-VA score of 2 or more is recommended as an indicator of elevated thromboembolic risk for decisions on initiating oral anticoagulation.
Oral anticoagulation is recommended in all patients with AF and hypertrophic cardiomyopathy or cardiac amyloidosis, regardless of CHA2DS2-VA score, to prevent ischaemic stroke and thromboembolism.
Individualized reassessment of thromboembolic risk is recommended at periodic intervals in patients with AF to ensure anticoagulation is started in appropriate patients.
Antiplatelet therapy is not recommended as an alternative to anticoagulation in patients with AF to prevent ischaemic stroke and thromboembolism.
Using the temporal pattern of clinical AF (paroxysmal, persistent, or permanent) is not recommended to determine the need for oral anticoagulation.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for oral anticoagulation in AF

rows.recommendation: Direct oral anticoagulants are recommended in preference to VKAs to prevent ischaemic stroke and thromboembolism, except in patients with mechanical heart valves or moderate-to-severe mitral stenosis.
A target INR of 2.0–3.0 is recommended for patients with AF prescribed a VKA for stroke prevention to ensure safety and effectiveness.

Switching to a DOAC is recommended for eligible patients that have failed to maintain an adequate time in therapeutic range on a VKA (TTR <70%) to prevent thromboembolism and intracranial haemorrhage.
A reduced dose of DOAC therapy is not recommended, unless patients meet DOAC-specific criteria, to prevent underdosing and avoidable thromboembolic events.

rows.recommendation: Amiodarone is recommended in patients with AF and HFrEF requiring long-term antiarrhythmic drug therapy to prevent recurrence and progression of AF, with careful consideration and monitoring for extracardiac toxicity.

Dronedarone is recommended in patients with AF requiring long-term rhythm control, including those with HFmrEF, HFpEF, ischaemic heart disease, or valvular disease to prevent recurrence and progression of AF.

Flecainide or propafenone is recommended in patients with AF requiring long-term rhythm control to prevent recurrence and progression of AF, excluding those with impaired left ventricular systolic function, severe left ventricular hypertrophy, or coronary artery disease.
Antiarrhythmic drug therapy is not recommended in patients with advanced conduction disturbances unless antibradycardia pacing is provided.

rows.recommendation: Antiplatelet therapy beyond 12 months is not recommended in stable patients with chronic coronary or vascular disease treated with oral anticoagulation, due to lack of efficacy and to avoid major bleeding.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for management of post-operative AF

rows.recommendation: Peri-operative amiodarone therapy is recommended where drug therapy is desired to prevent post-operative AF after cardiac surgery.
Routine use of beta-blockers is not recommended in patients undergoing non-cardiac surgery for the prevention of post-operative AF.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for patients with embolic stroke of unknown source

rows.recommendation: Prolonged monitoring for AF is recommended in patients with ESUS to inform on AF treatment decisions.
Initiation of oral anticoagulation in ESUS patients without documented AF is not recommended due to lack of efficacy in preventing ischaemic stroke and thromboembolism.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for patients with AF during pregnancy

rows.recommendation: Immediate electrical cardioversion is recommended in patients with AF during pregnancy and haemodynamic instability or pre-excited AF to improve maternal and foetal outcomes.

Therapeutic anticoagulation with LMWHs or VKAs (except VKAs for the first trimester or beyond Week 36) is recommended for pregnant patients with AF at elevated thromboembolic risk to prevent ischaemic stroke and thromboembolism.
Beta-1 selective blockers are recommended for heart rate control of AF in pregnancy to reduce symptoms and improve maternal and foetal outcomes, excluding atenolol.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for prevention of thromboembolism in atrial flutter

rows.recommendation: Oral anticoagulation is recommended in patients with atrial flutter at elevated thromboembolic risk to prevent ischaemic stroke and thromboembolism.
